analysis.one_liner: Eliminates mandatory minimum prison sentences for federal drug offenses.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote; it sat in two House committees until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would strike the mandatory minimum prison terms that Congress attached to federal drug crimes in the 1980s, letting judges set sentences based on each case instead of drug weight alone. It would also require the Attorney General's written approval before prosecutors bring low-quantity drug cases. It was referred to the Judiciary and Energy and Commerce committees, where it died without any action.
analysis.who_benefits: People facing federal drug charges, especially low-level offenders who currently face automatically long sentences set by drug weight rather than by their actual role. The bill's own findings note that more than half of drug trafficking offenders face a mandatory minimum, that most are nonviolent or low-level, and that these penalties fall disproportionately on Black and Hispanic defendants and on women in peripheral roles.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Federal drug defendants and their families

how_it_helps.text: Removes mandatory minimum sentences for trafficking, import/export, and simple possession offenses, letting judges sentence below the former floor and restoring parole-style discretion over the term of years [S3].

Requires the Attorney General's prior written approval to prosecute cases involving low drug quantities (for example, less than one kilogram of heroin or 500 grams of cocaine-based substances), which would push low-level cases out of federal court or force national-level sign-off [S3].

The bill's findings cite Sentencing Commission data that in fiscal year 2016 only about 29 percent of mandatory-minimum drug trafficking convictions involved a weapon or violence and fewer than 12 percent involved a leadership role, and that Black and Hispanic offenders make up roughly three-quarters of drug offenders sentenced [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal prosecutors and the Justice Department lose automatic leverage: mandatory minimums are the main tool for pressuring plea bargains, and the AG-approval gate adds a layer of review to low-level prosecutions. Anyone arguing that long automatic sentences deter trafficking bears the policy cost if those sentences are gone.

drawbacks.text: Mandatory minimums give prosecutors leverage to secure cooperation from major traffickers and remove judicial discretion that critics say can be too lenient; eliminating them for all quantities, including large-scale importation, goes further than the narrower reforms in the 2018 First Step Act [S3].
Centralizing prosecution decisions in the Attorney General's office for low-quantity cases makes federal drug charging dependent on the priorities of one political appointee [S3].

The bill did not advance in any committee, so it never faced scrutiny, amendments, or a cost estimate; its findings lean on data about nonviolent low-level offenders while the text applies to all drug trafficking quantities [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addresses a real, documented problem: decades-long automatic sentences for low-level drug offenders and sharp racial disparities, at a cost to taxpayers of roughly $36,000 per prisoner per year. The main honest objection is scope — it removes judicially unreviewable floors everywhere, including for high-quantity trafficking, rather than calibrating relief to low-level offenders. A narrower bill would likely have been easier to defend; this one never got the chance to be amended because it never received any committee action.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary and Energy and Commerce committees on the day it was introduced, and neither committee ever acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Maxine Waters introduced the bill on June 11, 2020, joined by five Democratic cosponsors: Reps. Schakowsky, Lee, Norton, Pocan, and Khanna [S3] [S4].
The same day, it was referred to the Committee on the Judiciary and, in addition, to the Committee on Energy and Commerce [S1] [S5].
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action appears in the bill's action history; the referred-committee stage is the last entry before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal prosecutors keep the sentencing leverage and the status quo of drug mandatory minimums; no one in federal prison benefits because the bill died in committee with only six sponsors and no committee action [S5].

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo: prosecutors keep mandatory minimums

for.name: Rep. Maxine Waters
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Mandatory Minimum Reform Act of 2020 on June 11, 2020

for.name: Reps. Schakowsky, Lee, Norton, Pocan, and Khanna

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.role: Chair of the committee of primary referral
against.what_they_did: The committee never held a hearing or markup, and no floor vote was ever scheduled; the referral was the last action on the bill

sides.party_line_note: All six sponsors were Democrats; no Republican cosponsored the bill and no committee or floor vote was ever taken [S4] [S5].

industries.note: Federal prison beds are a revenue source for private prison companies; eliminating mandatory minimums would shrink sentences and, over time, the prison population they are paid to house. Their interest runs against shorter sentences for drug defendants.

industries.industry: Federal prosecution and law enforcement agencies
industries.note: Prosecutors lose the automatic leverage that mandatory minimums provide in plea bargaining, and low-quantity prosecutions would need the Attorney General's sign-off. Not an industry in the commercial sense, but a concentrated institutional interest the bill curtails.
